transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, honestly, it’s just... it’s gotten to a point where I really needed to talk to someone. I’m an auditor, you see, and my job is all about details, follow-through, making sure every single box is checked. And I’ve been doing it a long time, but lately—or maybe it's always been this way and it's just catching up to me—I’m dropping the ball in the most frustrating ways. 

What really pushed me to finally make this appointment is this pattern I've noticed. I’ll wrap up an audit, or maybe one of the mentorship events I help run for the junior staff, and I’ll have this list of follow-up items. And I start them. I really do. I’ll sit down at my desk, open the files, get the emails drafted, with every intention of just knocking them out right then and there. I’m completely focused on getting it done. But then, I don't know, a few days will pass, and someone will ask me about a review note, or I'll go to check my outbox, and I realize the final email never actually went out. Or the form I spent an hour reviewing never got signed and submitted. It’s like I get 95% of the way there and then just... stop. And I don't even realize I've stopped until it's a problem. It's embarrassing, frankly, especially at my level. I just can't seem to push things across the actual finish line, no matter how much I intend to.
When you get stuck on these tasks, is it because you feel they have to be done perfectly before you can finish them?

No, no, I wouldn't say it's about perfectionism. I mean, as an auditor, you have to be accurate, obviously, but I don't sit there agonizing over whether the wording in an email is, you know, absolutely flawless or if the formatting on a spreadsheet is perfectly aligned before I send it. It's not that I'm paralyzed by trying to make it perfect. It's more like... I just sort of evaporate from the task. 

Like, I'll be sitting there, right? I've got the audit report open on my left monitor, the client's trial balance on the right, and I'm tying out the last few numbers. I know exactly what needs to be done. It's not even hard work at that point, it's just the final mechanical steps. And I'll think, "Okay, just need to attach this to the email to the partner for review." And I might even draft the email! "Hi David, attached is the final Q3 review for Smith & Co. Let me know if you have any questions." But then... maybe a notification pops up, or I remember I need to check if the junior staff submitted their timesheets, or honestly, sometimes nothing happens at all, my brain just kind of shifts gears without my permission. And the draft just sits there. 

I'm not holding it back because I think it needs more work. I genuinely, in that moment, feel like I *did* it. Or I fully intend to click send in five seconds, but those five seconds turn into three days. I don't have that feeling of, "Oh, this isn't good enough yet." It's more of a complete disconnect between the intention to finish and the physical act of finishing. Which is why it's so baffling to me! Because I know how to do my job, and I'm not afraid of doing it wrong. I just... wander away mentally right at the very end.
Were you having similar attention or follow-through problems as a child or teenager?

Oh, gosh, yes. Yes, absolutely. I mean, it’s actually kind of funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my mother about this the other day—well, not about this appointment specifically, I haven't told her I'm here, but just about how things used to be. And it's always been this way. Even way back in elementary school, I remember my report cards. Every single year, it was the same story. The teachers would always write these little notes, you know, "She's very bright," or "She understands the material quickly," but then there was always the "but." It was always, "but she loses her assignments," or "she rushes past the small details." 

I can't tell you how many times I would just completely skip over a whole section of a worksheet because I was in such a hurry to be done, or I'd miss a minus sign in math because I wasn't looking closely enough. And the talking! Oh, I was always getting in trouble for talking out of turn. I just had so much to say and I couldn't wait for the teacher to call on me. They were constantly having to remind me to finish my work, too. I'd start something, get distracted by what the kid next to me was doing, and completely forget what I was supposed to be working on. 

My mother, she still jokes about it to this day. She loves to tell this story at family gatherings about how I could completely ace a spelling test or a history quiz—like, literally get a hundred percent without even studying that hard—but then I would completely forget to turn in the big diorama project that was sitting right there in my backpack. I'd do all the work, build the whole thing, put it in my bag, take it to school, and then it would just... stay in the backpack. For weeks! Until it was crushed or my mom found it. So, yes, it’s definitely not a new thing, it’s just... the consequences are a lot bigger now than a crushed shoebox diorama, you know?
Do you currently find yourself feeling restless or having trouble sitting still?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It’s actually one of the things that makes my job so exhausting, to be completely honest with you. Because, you know, auditing is... well, it’s a lot of sitting. It’s hours and hours of sitting in front of a screen, or in a conference room, looking at spreadsheets and financial statements and just... sitting. 

And I try, I really do. I’ll settle into my chair, I’ll have my coffee, I’ll tell myself, "Okay, we are going to get through this quarterly review for the Smith account, and we are not going to move until it’s done." But then... it’s like this physical sensation. It’s not just in my head, it’s in my body. It’s like this pressure starts building up inside me, right in my chest or my legs, and it just gets tighter and tighter the longer I sit there. 

It gets to the point where sitting still actually feels physically uncomfortable. Like, I’ll start shifting my weight, crossing and uncrossing my legs, tapping my pen on the desk—which I know drives my colleagues crazy, but I almost can’t help it. And eventually, the pressure just gets to be too much, and I absolutely *have* to get up. I’ll invent any excuse. I’ll think, "Oh, I should go check if that document printed," even though I know perfectly well I haven't sent anything to the printer all morning. Or I’ll decide I urgently need to go fill my water bottle, or I’ll just walk a lap around the floor under the guise of going to the restroom. 

I just... I need to move. I have to release that built-up energy or pressure or whatever it is, otherwise I feel like I’m going to crawl out of my own skin. And then, of course, once I’m up and walking around, that’s when I run into someone in the hall, or I see something else that needs doing, and suddenly I’m completely derailed from the review I was supposed to be doing in the first place. So it’s this vicious cycle of trying to sit still, failing because it’s so uncomfortable, getting up to move, and then losing my focus entirely. It’s incredibly frustrating.
Do you also often interrupt people or blurt out answers before they finish speaking?

Oh, definitely. That is... yeah, that’s actually a really big problem for me, and it’s something I feel incredibly guilty about, to be honest. It’s like the thought just pops into my head and it is so loud and so... urgent. It just feels overwhelmingly urgent. If I don't get it out right that exact second, I feel like I'm going to either explode or completely lose the thought forever. 

I notice it the absolute most at work, especially when I'm dealing with the junior auditors. You know, the new hires who are just fresh out of college and still trying to figure out how everything works. They’ll come into my office or call me on Teams to ask a question about a workpaper, and they start explaining the issue, like, "Oh, I was looking at the revenue recognition for this client, and I noticed that the invoice—" and boom. I already know exactly what they're going to ask. I can see the whole trajectory of the conversation. And instead of just letting them finish their sentence, which is what a polite, professional manager is supposed to do, I just... I catch myself jumping right into the conversation. 

I’ll just blurt out, "You need to check the deferred revenue schedule from last year!" before they've even gotten to the actual question. It just comes flying out of my mouth before my brain can even hit the brakes. I literally blurt it out before I can stop myself. And then, of course, I feel terrible. I can see their faces kind of fall, or they look startled, and they lose their train of thought, and then I have to backtrack and apologize and say, "I'm so sorry, please, go ahead, finish what you were saying." 

But it is just so physically hard to wait. It's like my brain is moving at a hundred miles an hour and they're speaking at twenty, and I just want to fast-forward the conversation to the conclusion. My husband complains about it all the time, too, to be fair. We'll be talking about our weekend plans and I'll just talk right over him because an idea popped into my head. But at work, with the juniors, it really bothers me because I don't want to come across as condescending or impatient, but that urgency just takes over completely. It’s like a reflex I have zero control over.
Do these attention and follow-through problems cause you significant problems in more than one area of your life, such as at work and at home?

Oh, yes. Yes, it’s everywhere. It’s not just one area, it’s bleeding into absolutely everything, and that’s honestly the main reason I finally made this appointment. It’s just become too much to manage on my own. 

At work, it’s... well, it’s getting really bad. As an auditor, you have to be meticulous, obviously, but my mistakes, these careless little errors, and my unfinished follow-ups... they've just piled up. It actually reached a breaking point recently where an entire client review was affected. I had promised to follow up on some missing documentation for a major account, and I got sidetracked by another project, and I just completely dropped the ball. The partner had to step in at the eleventh hour to smooth things over with the client, and it was so humiliating. And the worst part is, I’m supposed to be up for a promotion to senior manager soon. But now I’m constantly worrying, like, I can literally feel people looking at me and questioning whether I can actually handle the promotion. I mean, if I can't even follow through on a basic client review without someone having to rescue me, how am I supposed to manage a larger portfolio? It just keeps me up at night, running through all the things I might have forgotten to do that day.

And then I go home, hoping I can just relax, but it’s honestly just as much of a disaster there. My husband, bless him, he has completely had to take over the household management. I used to be in charge of the bills—which is incredibly ironic, right? An accountant who can't manage to pay her own water bill on time. But I’d open the mail, set the envelopes on the kitchen counter to pay "later," and then completely forget they existed until we got late notices or the internet got shut off. He finally just took all the accounts over because he couldn't take the stress of it. 

And it’s not just the financial stuff. It’s everyday commitments, too. I’ll agree to handle something, like calling the contractor about the roof, or organizing a dinner with our friends, and I just... don't do it. I mean well, I really do intend to do it when I agree to it, but he just cannot count on me to complete things reliably anymore. He actually told me last week that he just assumes if he doesn't do a task himself, it won't get done. And hearing that from your spouse... it just breaks your heart, you know? It makes you feel like a complete failure on every single front. So, yes, to answer your question, it is definitely causing major, major problems in both my professional and personal life.
